The last 88 pulses, one burst at a time

2026-08-16 · follows the anatomy of the unmatched and the matching audit · live numbers on the match QA page

279,938 of 279,972 matchable pulses since run_79 are now confidently matched — 99.99 % at the 60 % per-pulse bar. Of the 88 that were left after the 15 August mop-up, 25 were recovered by pairing each burst with each candidate n_TOF bunch by exhaustion, 260 pulses of a sub-run that had no n_TOF run proposed over it were shown to be a stretch where n_TOF was simply not recording (no run 224649 or 224650 exists anywhere on the DAQ tree), and everything still unmatched is either a partial burst of 11–14 triggers with no partner hits anywhere in ±120 s × ±100 ms (3 pulses) or a cluster of fewer than 10 triggers recorded while no beam burst was — noise, not a pulse (31). n_TOF was not recording for 1,516 of 281,488 beam pulses DREAM triggered on (0.54 %), reported separately as before.

Why a per-burst scan, and why it works

The production chain locks a whole sub-run at once: pulse_match enumerates candidate offsets from a 50 ms cluster count, the coincidence arbiter measures each on 32 sampled pulses, the clock is fitted on the segment. Every step needs statistics a lone burst does not have — which is exactly where the last unmatched pulses were: 6 or 17 real bursts at the tail of a sub-run after the beam stopped, or one burst inside a matched sub-run whose assigned bunch showed no coincidence. Nothing in the chain could ask, of a single burst, which bunch, at which offset, holds its partner hits? slim_pipeline/burst_bruteforce.py asks it by trying all of them.

For a burst with triggers ti (DREAM ns since its flash) and a bunch with wall-AND-plastic singles candidates ck (n_TOF ns since its flash), every difference ck − ti(1+K) is histogrammed at 2 µs over ±100 ms. At the right pairing the ~90 triggers of a beam pulse pile into one bin (the burst shares one T0, and the seed rate ratio K is good to ~2 µs over the 80 ms gate). A wrong pairing is not flat — both time series are dense in the same places (the flash region, the thermal peak) and a wrong bunch still puts ~0.4 of the triggers into its tallest bin — so the coarse peak only chooses who gets refined, and the decision is made at 20 ns: a per-burst (da, dk) line on the core residuals, exactly as clockfit.fit_perbunch does, then the fraction of triggers with a candidate inside ±25 ns. That is the same per-pulse coincidence fraction the ledger uses, so a burst this tool calls matched is matched by the production definition. It separates cleanly: of the 71 bursts scanned, the 65 with a partner scored 71–99 % at the winning bunch (one control at 59 %) against 2–6 % at the runner-up; the six without one (three stubs, run_82's three post-run bursts) never got past 3 %. Blind controls — eight bursts per sub-run that the production join had already placed — were re-found at their known bunch every time; their fitted intercepts (T0 + da, MAD 2–9 ns) are the reference against which a target's flash offset is measured.

Cost: one condor job per n_TOF run (the run is staged to node scratch, ~30 GB), 25 s to 6 min of scanning per sub-run over 47–162 bunches. Overkill for 88 pulses, and the point.

Two things worth keeping from this beyond the count. First, the ~1 ms class: three independent bursts in three sub-runs, each with its DREAM time base referenced to a trigger 0.997–1.040 ms after the flash — the N93B gate's opening — is a DAQ signature (a dropped flash trigger), and it is now detectable in the products by construction: a burst whose per-bunch fit fails while its neighbours' succeed, and whose brute-force lag is +1 ms. Second, the two sub-run tails were never a small-sample fitting problem, as the earlier diagnosis assumed. The clock fit's peak at the right lock is 242–275 counts, above the 150 floor; what failed was upstream — the arbiter was never offered that lock. The floor was lowered for these two segments anyway (recorded as fit.bootstrap.min_peak), and it did not matter.

How the fixes reach the products

Every override lives in one file beside the pipeline, ntof_processing/slim_pipeline/burst_fixes.json, with the scan numbers that established it, and is applied by the production slim itself (slim_run.py / run_segment.py load it by default; slim.apply_fixes puts a segment's entry on the Segment; slim.apply_burst_fix applies per-burst entries to the joined events before anything downstream sees them). A whole-segment lock becomes accept_offset_s with source bruteforce. A per-burst entry moves the burst's events to the coinciding bunch and/or adds the flash shift to t_since_flash_ns (converted from the n_TOF time base the scan measures it in to DREAM ns — dividing by 1 + K, which for the 4.38 ms shift is a 482 ns difference and the reason the first attempt at run_102/0002 missed); triggers that then sit within 1 µs of the true flash are re-tagged as the flash and get no hits, like every other flash. The product records what was done in calibration.json → join.burst_fix and in burst_map.json → fix, with the burst's original bunch, so a fixed burst stays distinguishable from one the join placed on its own. The seven re-made products replaced their earlier vintages on EOS (publish_missing.py --replace, the only path that ever overwrites a root there); the 448 others are untouched.

What this does not settle

  • The 31 clusters of fewer than 10 triggers (run_137/0000's 19, run_145/0003's 11, one in run_139/0010) are counted in the denominator as unmatched. They are noise coincidences recorded while no beam burst was, not pulses; whether they belong out of the denominator with the empty pulses is a bookkeeping choice, and it moves the headline from 99.988 to 99.999 %.
  • The three 11–14-trigger stubs. A DREAM sub-run's first burst recorded mid-gate can be re-referenced when enough of it exists (run_102/0002's 88 triggers were); at 11–14 triggers no bunch stands out. They could only be recovered by relaxing the coincidence bar for a fragment, which would not be the same claim as "matched".
  • Whether the dropped-flash signature (+1 ms) occurs in bursts that are matched — a burst whose flash was dropped but whose per-bunch fit still landed would have absorbed the ~1 ms into a wrong da. The three found here all failed their fit; a scan of the per-bunch da distribution across the campaign would say whether any survived it.
